article.title: Messages are accepted but not arriving
article.excerpt: Every call returns success. Work through this in order — the first four checks do not involve the carrier at all.

p: Each step either finds the cause or rules out a whole layer, so a wrong guess early costs more than it saves.

steps.p: suppressed means the platform never tried to send it, and no provider investigation will help.
Transactional traffic must declare INFORMATIONAL or TRANSACTIONAL, or a recipient who opted out will have it suppressed.
If you never configured a callback URL, you will never learn that a message failed after submission.
If you retried after a timeout, there may be two messages, and the second one may be the one the recipient sees.

steps.h: Only then look at the provider
steps.p: Segments, encoding and errorCode on the failed message tell you whether this is an encoding, routing or carrier-side problem.

p: The send endpoint accepts asynchronously. Returning success means the platform submitted the message to the provider, and at that moment it may already have gone out.

So a client-side timeout is not evidence of failure. There is no idempotency key: resending produces a genuinely second message, sent and billed. If you do not have a messageId, look the send up in the console by time window and recipient number instead of resending it.

sections.h: A message that says delivered and was still not seen
p: delivered is the provider's report that the handset received the message, which is as far as any platform can see. It does not prove a human read it. Before treating it as a platform fault, confirm the recipient has not filtered the sending number, and that the message did not land in a filtered or spam view.
